steps.observation: You have 60 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Here’s a high-level, one-minute sketch of a Transformer:

1. Input Representation  
   • Each token (word, subword) is mapped to a fixed-length embedding.  
   • Positional encodings (sine/cosine or learned) are added so the model knows token order.

2. Self-Attention  
   • For each token, compute three vectors—Query (Q), Key (K), Value (V)—via learned linear projections.  
   • Attention scores = softmax( Q·Kᵀ / √d ) give weights for how much each other token should contribute.  
   • Multiply weights × V and sum to produce a new, context-aware representation for each token.

3. Multi-Head Attention  
   • Run several independent self-attention “heads” in parallel (each with its own Q/K/V projections).  
   • Concatenate their outputs and linearly project back, letting the model attend to different aspects of context.

4. Feed-Forward & Residuals  
   • After attention comes a position-wise feed-forward network (two linear layers with a nonlinearity).  
   • Residual connections + layer normalization wrap both the attention block and the feed-forward block to ease training.

5. Stacking Layers  
   • You stack N identical layers (often 6–24). Each layer refines the token representations further.

6. Encoder-Decoder (for sequence-to-sequence)  
   • Encoder: a stack of self-attention + feed-forward blocks processes the source.  
   • Decoder: has masked self-attention (to prevent peeking ahead) plus cross-attention over encoder outputs, then feed-forward.

Outcome: Tokens get continuously refined, learning which parts of the sequence matter most. That’s the core of the Transformer.
